questions.question: Which subatomic particle has a negative electric charge?
questions.explanation: An electron carries a negative elementary charge.

questions.question: Which subatomic particle has no electric charge?
The atomic number of an element equals its number of what?
questions.explanation: Atomic number is defined as the number of protons in the nucleus.

questions.question: The mass number of an atom is the total number of what?
questions.explanation: Mass number equals proton number plus neutron number.

questions.question: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of what?
questions.explanation: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with differing neutron numbers.

questions.question: Which model describes electrons occupying quantised energy levels around a nucleus?
questions.explanation: The Bohr model introduced discrete electron energy levels.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of electrons in the first principal energy level?
questions.explanation: The first shell has n = 1, so its capacity is 2n² = 2.

questions.question: What is the electronic configuration of sodium (atomic number 11) by shells?
questions.explanation: Sodium has 11 electrons arranged as 2, 8 and 1 in shells.

questions.question: Which particle determines the identity of an element?
questions.explanation: Changing the number of protons changes the atomic number and element.

questions.question: What is a positive ion formed when an atom loses electrons called?
questions.explanation: Loss of negatively charged electrons leaves a net positive charge.

questions.question: Elements in the same group of the periodic table generally have the same number of what?
questions.explanation: For main-group elements, group position relates to valence-electron count.

questions.question: Across a period from left to right, atomic radius generally does what?
questions.explanation: Increasing nuclear charge attracts electrons more strongly across a period.

questions.question: Which group contains the noble gases?
questions.explanation: Noble gases occupy Group 18 in the modern periodic table.

questions.question: Which element is an alkali metal?
questions.explanation: Potassium is a Group 1 alkali metal.

questions.question: Which element is a halogen?
questions.explanation: Bromine is a reactive Group 17 halogen.

questions.question: What is the general trend in metallic character down a group?
questions.explanation: Atoms tend to lose electrons more readily as size and shielding increase down a group.

questions.question: Which of these is a transition metal?
questions.explanation: Iron is a d-block transition metal.

questions.question: Which element has the chemical symbol K?
questions.explanation: K is the symbol for potassium, from the Latin name kalium.

questions.question: What type of bond forms when atoms share pairs of electrons?
questions.explanation: Covalent bonding involves shared electron pairs.

questions.question: What type of bond is formed by electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions?
questions.explanation: Ionic bonding involves attraction between cations and anions.

questions.question: Which substance contains predominantly ionic bonding?
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride consists of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in a lattice.

questions.question: Which molecule contains a double covalent bond?
questions.explanation: Each oxygen atom shares two pairs of electrons in O₂.

questions.question: Why do many ionic compounds have high melting points?
options: Strong electrostatic attractions hold their ions in a lattice
Their ions move freely in the solid
questions.answer: Strong electrostatic attractions hold their ions in a lattice
questions.explanation: A large amount of energy is needed to overcome the ionic lattice attractions.

questions.question: What is the shape of a methane molecule, CH₄?
questions.explanation: Four bonding pairs around carbon arrange tetrahedrally.

questions.question: What is the approximate bond angle in a tetrahedral molecule?
questions.explanation: The ideal tetrahedral bond angle is about 109.5 degrees.

questions.question: What is a polar covalent bond?
options: A covalent bond with unequal sharing of electrons
A bond with no electron interaction
A bond formed only between metals
A bond with complete electron transfer in every case
questions.answer: A covalent bond with unequal sharing of electrons
questions.explanation: Different electronegativities can make the shared electron pair unevenly distributed.

questions.question: Which intermolecular force is especially important between water molecules?
questions.explanation: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds because H is bonded to highly electronegative oxygen.

questions.question: What holds positive metal ions together in a metal lattice?
questions.explanation: Metallic bonding is attraction between metal cations and delocalised electrons.

questions.question: Which molecule is non-polar overall despite having polar bonds?
questions.explanation: The linear CO₂ molecule is symmetrical, so its bond dipoles cancel.

questions.question: Which substance is a giant covalent structure?
questions.explanation: Diamond has a three-dimensional network of covalent bonds.

questions.question: What is the SI unit for amount of substance?
questions.explanation: The mole is the SI unit for amount of substance.

questions.question: What is the approximate Avogadro constant?
questions.explanation: One mole contains approximately 6.022 × 10²³ specified entities.

questions.question: What is the molar mass of water, H₂O?
What does a balanced chemical equation conserve?
options: The number of molecules on each side always
questions.explanation: Balancing ensures the same number of atoms of each element on both sides.

questions.question: What is the coefficient ratio for H₂ and O₂ in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O?
questions.explanation: The balanced equation uses two moles of H₂ for every mole of O₂.

questions.question: What is the empirical formula of a compound?
options: The exact number of atoms in one molecule
The total mass of the compound
The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms
questions.answer: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms
questions.explanation: An empirical formula expresses the simplest integer atom ratio.

questions.question: What is the molar volume of an ideal gas at STP often approximated as?
questions.explanation: At 0 °C and 1 atm, an ideal gas occupies about 22.4 dm³ per mole.

questions.question: Which law states that matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction?
questions.explanation: In a closed system, total mass remains constant during chemical reactions.

questions.question: What is the limiting reactant?
options: The product with the smallest molar mass
The reactant with the largest mass always
The reactant consumed first that limits product formed
questions.answer: The reactant consumed first that limits product formed
questions.explanation: The limiting reactant determines the maximum theoretical product amount.

questions.question: What is the percentage yield formula?
questions.explanation: Percentage yield compares actual product with theoretical maximum.

questions.question: According to Brønsted–Lowry theory, an acid is a proton what?
According to Brønsted–Lowry theory, a base is a proton what?
What is the pH of a neutral aqueous solution at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: At 25 °C, a neutral solution has equal H⁺ and OH⁻ concentrations and pH 7.

questions.question: Which indicator is commonly used to distinguish acids and alkalis by colour change?
questions.explanation: Litmus turns red in acidic solution and blue in alkaline solution.

questions.question: What salt is produced when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide?
What gas is commonly released when dilute acids react with reactive metals?
questions.explanation: Many reactive metals displace hydrogen from dilute acids.

questions.question: What gas is released when an acid reacts with a carbonate?
questions.explanation: Acid + carbonate produces a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Which salt is formed from nitric acid?
What is neutralisation?
options: Reaction of an acid with a base to form salt and usually water
Dissolving a gas in water only
questions.answer: Reaction of an acid with a base to form salt and usually water
questions.explanation: Neutralisation commonly forms salt and water from acid and base.

questions.question: Which substance is amphoteric?
questions.explanation: Aluminium oxide can react with both acids and bases.

questions.question: Oxidation can be defined as loss of what?
questions.explanation: In electron-transfer terms, oxidation is loss of electrons.

questions.question: Reduction can be defined as gain of what?
In a galvanic cell, oxidation occurs at which electrode?
questions.explanation: Oxidation occurs at the anode in both galvanic and electrolytic cells.

questions.question: During electrolysis, positive ions move toward which electrode?
questions.explanation: Cations are attracted to the negatively charged cathode in an electrolytic cell.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a salt bridge in a galvanic cell?
options: To supply electrons directly to the circuit
To maintain electrical neutrality by ion movement
To increase electrode mass in all cases
questions.answer: To maintain electrical neutrality by ion movement
questions.explanation: The salt bridge permits ion flow that maintains charge balance.

questions.question: What is the oxidation number of oxygen in most compounds?
questions.explanation: Oxygen commonly has oxidation state −2, with notable exceptions such as peroxides.

questions.question: What happens to the oxidation number of an element when it is oxidised?
questions.explanation: Oxidation corresponds to electron loss and an increase in oxidation number.

questions.question: What is the product at the cathode when molten sodium chloride is electrolysed?
questions.explanation: Na⁺ gains electrons at the cathode to form sodium metal.

questions.question: What is the product at the anode when molten sodium chloride is electrolysed?
questions.explanation: Cl⁻ loses electrons at the anode, producing chlorine.

questions.question: What is corrosion of iron commonly called?
questions.explanation: Rusting is the electrochemical corrosion of iron in the presence of oxygen and moisture.

questions.question: What is a catalyst?
options: A product that stops all reactions
A substance that increases reaction rate without being consumed overall
A substance that changes equilibrium constant at fixed temperature
A reactant always used up completely
questions.answer: A substance that increases reaction rate without being consumed overall
questions.explanation: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy.

questions.question: How does increasing temperature usually affect reaction rate?
options: It has no effect on any reaction
questions.explanation: Higher temperature increases the fraction of collisions with sufficient energy.

questions.question: What is activation energy?
options: Total energy of all products only
Mass needed to start a reaction
Minimum energy required for a successful reaction pathway
questions.answer: Minimum energy required for a successful reaction pathway
questions.explanation: Reacting particles need sufficient energy to reach the transition state.

questions.question: For a reversible reaction at dynamic equilibrium, what is true?
options: Forward and reverse reaction rates are equal
Reactant and product concentrations must be equal
questions.answer: Forward and reverse reaction rates are equal
questions.explanation: At dynamic equilibrium, opposing rates are equal while concentrations remain constant.

questions.question: What does increasing pressure favour in a gaseous equilibrium, all else equal?
options: The side with more gas molecules
The side with fewer moles of gas
questions.answer: The side with fewer moles of gas
questions.explanation: Le Chatelier's principle predicts a shift toward fewer gas moles when pressure increases.

questions.question: What is the equilibrium constant changed by?
questions.explanation: For a given reaction, the equilibrium constant depends on temperature.

questions.question: What is the effect of a catalyst on the equilibrium position?
options: It does not change the equilibrium position
It changes K at constant temperature
questions.answer: It does not change the equilibrium position
questions.explanation: A catalyst speeds both forward and reverse reactions without changing K.

questions.question: Which factor commonly increases the rate of a reaction between solids and liquids?
questions.explanation: Greater surface area exposes more particles for effective collisions.

questions.question: What is an exothermic reaction?
options: A reaction that absorbs heat only
A reaction with no energy change
A reaction that releases heat to its surroundings
A reaction that cannot occur spontaneously
questions.answer: A reaction that releases heat to its surroundings
questions.explanation: Exothermic reactions transfer energy outward, often raising surroundings' temperature.

questions.question: For an endothermic reaction, the enthalpy change ΔH is generally what sign?
questions.explanation: Endothermic reactions absorb heat, so products have higher enthalpy than reactants.

questions.question: What is the general formula of open-chain alkanes?
questions.explanation: A saturated acyclic alkane has formula CnH2n+2.

questions.question: What type of hydrocarbon contains at least one carbon–carbon double bond?
questions.explanation: Alkenes contain a C=C double bond.

questions.question: What is the molecular formula of methane?
questions.explanation: Methane is the simplest alkane, with one carbon bonded to four hydrogen atoms.

questions.question: Which functional group defines alcohols?
questions.explanation: Alcohols contain a hydroxyl group attached to a saturated carbon.

questions.question: Which functional group defines carboxylic acids?
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group –COOH.

questions.question: What is the product of complete combustion of a hydrocarbon in excess oxygen?
questions.explanation: Complete combustion oxidises carbon to CO₂ and hydrogen to H₂O.

questions.question: What is the name of the two-carbon alkane?
questions.explanation: Ethane contains two carbon atoms and formula C₂H₆.

questions.question: What is the name of the two-carbon alkene?
questions.explanation: Ethene contains a C=C bond and has formula C₂H₄.

questions.question: What is polymerisation?
options: Joining many small molecules into a large molecule
questions.answer: Joining many small molecules into a large molecule

questions.question: Which polymer is commonly made by addition polymerisation of ethene?
questions.explanation: Ethene monomers add across their double bonds to form poly(ethene).

questions.question: What is the chemical formula of ammonia?
questions.explanation: Ammonia contains one nitrogen and three hydrogen atoms.

questions.question: What is the chemical formula of sulfuric acid?
questions.explanation: Sulfuric acid has the formula H₂SO₄.

questions.question: What is the formula of calcium carbonate?
questions.explanation: Calcium carbonate consists of Ca²⁺ and CO₃²⁻.

questions.question: Which gas turns limewater milky?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide forms insoluble calcium carbonate in limewater.

questions.question: Which gas relights a glowing splint?
questions.explanation: Oxygen supports combustion and relights a glowing splint.

questions.question: Which gas gives a squeaky pop when ignited in a suitable test?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen burns rapidly with a characteristic pop in the standard test.

questions.question: Which gas has a pungent smell and turns damp red litmus paper blue?
questions.explanation: Ammonia is alkaline and turns damp red litmus blue.

questions.question: What is the principal ore of aluminium?
questions.explanation: Bauxite is the main commercial source of aluminium.

questions.question: What is the main constituent of natural gas?
questions.explanation: Natural gas consists mainly of methane, though composition varies.

questions.question: Which oxide is acidic?
questions.explanation: Sulfur dioxide is a non-metal oxide that forms an acidic solution in water.

questions.question: Which method separates an insoluble solid from a liquid?
questions.explanation: Filtration retains insoluble particles while liquid passes through the filter.

questions.question: Which method separates miscible liquids with different boiling points?
questions.explanation: Fractional distillation separates miscible liquids based on boiling-point differences.

questions.question: Which method is useful for separating coloured dyes in ink?
questions.explanation: Dyes travel different distances due to different affinities for stationary and mobile phases.

questions.question: What is crystallisation commonly used for?
options: Obtaining a pure solid from its solution
Turning a metal into a polymer
questions.answer: Obtaining a pure solid from its solution
questions.explanation: Crystallisation forms solid crystals as solvent is removed or solution cools.

questions.question: What is the purpose of using a boiling chip in a suitable heating setup?
options: To increase the mass of vapour
To act as a catalyst in every reaction
questions.explanation: Boiling chips provide nucleation sites and help reduce bumping.

questions.question: In paper chromatography, what does a high Rf value mean?
options: The sample must be pure water
The spot travelled a large fraction of the solvent-front distance
questions.answer: The spot travelled a large fraction of the solvent-front distance
questions.explanation: Rf = distance travelled by spot divided by distance travelled by solvent front.

questions.question: Which gas is a major contributor to the enhanced greenhouse effect?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide absorbs infrared radiation and contributes to warming.

questions.question: Which substance is a major cause of acid rain when released from combustion processes?
questions.explanation: Sulfur dioxide can oxidise and form acids in atmospheric moisture.

questions.question: What is eutrophication often caused by?
options: Removal of all nutrients from soil
questions.explanation: Excess nitrates and phosphates can trigger algal growth and oxygen depletion.

questions.question: Which practice helps reduce plastic waste?
options: Using single-use plastics for every task
questions.explanation: Reuse and suitable recycling reduce the amount of plastic entering the environment.

questions.question: What should be done first if a chemical splashes into the eyes in a laboratory?
options: Add another chemical to neutralise it
Rinse immediately with plenty of clean running water and alert the supervisor
questions.answer: Rinse immediately with plenty of clean running water and alert the supervisor
questions.explanation: Immediate prolonged rinsing and prompt assistance are standard first-aid responses.

questions.question: Why should chemicals never be tasted in a laboratory?
options: All chemicals are edible in small amounts
Taste is a reliable purity test
They may be toxic or corrosive
questions.answer: They may be toxic or corrosive
questions.explanation: Unknown chemicals can cause poisoning or injury.

questions.question: What does a fume cupboard help control?
options: Exposure to hazardous vapours and gases
questions.answer: Exposure to hazardous vapours and gases
questions.explanation: A fume cupboard removes or contains hazardous airborne substances.

questions.question: Why should acid generally be added to water rather than water to concentrated acid?
options: Water always explodes on contact with acid
Dilution can release heat and adding water may cause dangerous splashing
questions.answer: Dilution can release heat and adding water may cause dangerous splashing
questions.explanation: Adding acid slowly to water helps dissipate heat and reduces splashing risk.

questions.question: What is the Haber process used to manufacture?
questions.explanation: The Haber process combines nitrogen and hydrogen to make ammonia.

questions.question: What is the Contact process used to manufacture?
questions.explanation: The Contact process produces sulfuric acid from sulfur dioxide via sulfur trioxide.

questions.question: Which catalyst is commonly used in the Haber process?
questions.explanation: Finely divided iron is the usual industrial Haber-process catalyst.

questions.question: Which catalyst is commonly used in the Contact process oxidation of SO₂?
questions.explanation: Vanadium(V) oxide catalyses oxidation of sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide.

questions.question: What is cracking in petroleum processing?
options: Combining all hydrocarbons into one giant molecule
Breaking large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller molecules
questions.answer: Breaking large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller molecules
questions.explanation: Cracking converts heavier hydrocarbons into smaller alkanes and alkenes.

questions.question: Why is fractional distillation used in crude oil refining?
options: It converts all hydrocarbons into metals
All components have identical boiling points
questions.explanation: Components condense at different levels according to boiling range.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a spectator ion?
options: An ion that acts as a catalyst in every reaction
An ion that always forms a gas
An ion unchanged in the overall ionic reaction
An ion that is never dissolved
questions.answer: An ion unchanged in the overall ionic reaction
questions.explanation: Spectator ions appear unchanged on both sides of the complete ionic equation.

questions.question: Which pH value represents the most acidic solution?
questions.explanation: Lower pH indicates greater hydrogen-ion activity in ordinary dilute aqueous solutions.

questions.question: What is the usual colour of phenolphthalein in an alkaline solution?
questions.explanation: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in alkaline solution.

questions.question: In electrolysis, what happens to cations at the cathode?
questions.explanation: Cations are reduced by gaining electrons at the cathode.

questions.question: Which change usually increases the frequency of effective collisions?
options: Lowering temperature in an endothermic collision model
questions.explanation: Higher concentration usually increases collision frequency per unit volume.

questions.question: What is the characteristic reaction of an alkene with bromine water?
options: It turns bromine water deep blue
questions.explanation: The C=C bond undergoes addition with bromine, removing its orange-brown colour.

questions.question: Which test is commonly used to distinguish a carboxylic acid from an alcohol?
options: Add water and check whether either freezes
Add sodium hydrogencarbonate and observe effervescence
Measure the colour of a dry sample only
questions.answer: Add sodium hydrogencarbonate and observe effervescence
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids react with hydrogencarbonate to release CO₂; ordinary alcohols do not.

questions.question: What is the oxidation state of sulfur in H₂SO₄?
Which technique can separate a soluble solid from a solution while recovering the solvent?
questions.explanation: Distillation vaporises and then condenses the solvent, leaving solute behind.

questions.question: Which gas is associated with incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels and is poisonous?
questions.explanation: Incomplete combustion can produce toxic carbon monoxide, which interferes with oxygen transport in blood.

questions.question: Why is ammonia synthesis carried out at elevated pressure?
options: It converts nitrogen directly into oxygen
It favours the side with fewer gas molecules
It removes the need for a catalyst
It makes the equilibrium constant independent of temperature
questions.answer: It favours the side with fewer gas molecules
questions.explanation: The Haber reaction reduces gas moles from four to two, so higher pressure favours ammonia.

questions.question: What should be done before using a chemical reagent?
options: Assume it is harmless if colourless
Mix it with an unknown reagent
Read its label and relevant safety instructions
questions.answer: Read its label and relevant safety instructions
questions.explanation: Labels and safety information identify hazards and handling precautions.
